text:
**Short answer:** Pick a power station with at least **1,800 W of continuous AC output**. For most people, I'd recommend the **BLUETTI Elite 200 V2**.

**Top pick: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 ($899)**
- It has a 2,600 W inverter and 2,073.6 Wh of capacity. That gives you headroom to run an 1,800 W induction plate at full power, with enough battery for repeated cooking ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop)).
- Dealectric lists it as in stock. It also says 1,800 W stations such as the AC180 and DELTA 3 Plus run a plate "at its limit", so the Elite 200 V2 has more margin.
- Buy link: [BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2). Dealectric says the code DEALECTRIC takes $44.95 off, and the link applies it automatically. That page is also the retailer's own listing, so treat its "in stock" and "headroom" claims as the seller's.

**Why wattage matters more than battery size**
- A single-burner induction cooktop such as the Duxtop 9100MC is rated 1,800 W at its top setting, and its lower settings draw less ([HomePowerFacts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/)).
- A station with a smaller inverter can't run it on high, however big its battery is. Small units like the EcoFlow RIVER 3 (300 W continuous) and the 300 Wh class (300–600 W) can't run it ([HomePowerFacts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/), [BlackoutWise](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop)).
- The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 stops at 1,500 W, so it can shut off if you turn the burner to high ([BlackoutWise](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop)).
- Many cheap plates get "low" heat by switching 1,200 W on and off. Your inverter still sees 1,200 W peaks, so size for that ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop)).

**How long it will run**
- A 1,000 Wh-class unit cooks for about 45–50 minutes, and a 2,000 Wh unit for about 1.5 hours ([BlackoutWise](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop)). That assumes the burner averages about 1,080 W as it cycles.
- At a constant 1,800 W, a 2,000 Wh-class station lasts roughly an hour ([PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop)).
- A 15-minute one-pot meal at 1,200 W uses about 300 Wh. That's roughly 6–7 such meals from a 2 kWh station ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop)). That figure is my arithmetic from their numbers, and it ignores the roughly 10% inverter loss they mention, so expect a bit fewer.

**Electric kettle**
- Boiling a litre takes only about 90–110 Wh ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop)). A 1 kWh station could manage roughly eight boils.
- The results I found don't give kettle wattages. Check your kettle's rating against the station's continuous output. Many kettles draw about 1,500 W, but that's from my own knowledge, not these results.

**Tips to stretch the battery**
- Boil at full power, then drop to 400–800 W to simmer. Induction responds instantly. Cooking a whole meal at level 5–6 instead of max can roughly halve the energy used ([PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop)).
- Keep the station's vents clear. Running at 1,500–1,800 W for long stretches makes it hot, and it may cut output if it overheats ([VanLifeKitchens](https://vanlifekitchens.com/guides/can-a-power-station-run-an-induction-cooktop)).

**Other options**
- If you only need the DJI Power 1000, it's the smallest model HomePowerFacts found that can run a single burner. But it lasts only about 0.4 h on a full charge ([HomePowerFacts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/)).
- For longer cooking, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra (about 3 h) and the 4,096 Wh DELTA Pro 3 (about 3 h) are the longest-running options in the results. Prices weren't listed.
